note: Journey times are from Gare du Nord or Gare de l'Est unless stated — both are a short walk from home, which is a real advantage. Add ~10 min to reach the station. Check times on sncf-connect.com or transilien.com before you go.

items.title: Chantilly
items.transit: Gare du Nord → Chantilly-Gouvieux, ~25 min direct, then a 20-min walk through the park
items.why: The best value day trip you have, and almost nobody in Paris realises it is twenty-five minutes from Gare du Nord. A moated château holding the second-best collection of old master paintings in France after the Louvre, the grandest stables ever built for horses, a Le Nôtre park you can row a boat on, and the village where crème Chantilly was invented — you can eat it in the château's own dairy. Go early, come back for dinner.

stops.text: Gare du Nord to Chantilly-Gouvieux, 25 minutes
The château and the Musée Condé paintings
The Great Stables and the horse museum
Crème Chantilly at the Hameau in the park
A rowing boat on the Grand Canal

items.season: All year; the park is best from April to October. The château is shut on Tuesdays.

items.title: Reims & the Champagne Cellars
items.priceNote: ~€50 return TGV if booked early + tastings from €25
items.transit: Gare de l'Est → Reims by TGV, about 46 min
items.why: Champagne is forty-six minutes from Gare de l'Est. Reims has a UNESCO cathedral where the kings of France were crowned, and beneath the city are kilometres of Roman chalk quarries now used as champagne cellars — Taittinger and Ruinart both run tours that end in a tasting. Book the cellar tour and the TGV a few weeks ahead and this costs less than a nice dinner in Paris.

stops.text: TGV from Gare de l’Est, 46 minutes
The cathedral of the coronations, and its Chagall windows
A cellar tour in the chalk — Taittinger or Ruinart, booked
The Palais du Tau next to the cathedral
A last glass on the Place Drouet-d’Erlon

items.season: All year; the harvest is in September, and the cellars are cool in summer.

items.title: Vaux-le-Vicomte by Candlelight
items.transit: Gare de Lyon → Verneuil-l'Étang (~35 min), then the Châteaubus shuttle
items.why: The château that made Louis XIV so jealous he had its owner arrested and hired the same team to build Versailles. On Saturday evenings from May to early October they light two thousand candles through the house and gardens and you walk round in the dark. It is the most romantic thing within an hour of Paris and it is far less known than it should be. Check their site for candlelight dates before booking.

stops.text: Gare de Lyon to Verneuil-l’Étang and the Châteaubus
The house, and the dome
The gardens down to the Hercules statue
On candlelight Saturdays, stay after dark for the two thousand candles

items.season: Late March to early November. Candlelight evenings are Saturdays from May to early October.

items.title: Provins
items.transit: Gare de l'Est → Provins direct, about 1h25
items.why: A complete walled medieval town, UNESCO-listed, reachable on a single direct train from Gare de l'Est. Ramparts you can walk along, underground tunnels dug by merchants in the 12th century, and, in summer, falconry displays and jousting that are much better than that sounds. Go on a day when you want to be somewhere that feels nothing like Paris.

stops.text: Gare de l’Est to Provins, direct
The ramparts and the Porte Saint-Jean
The underground tunnels, by guided visit
The Tour César at the top of the town
The falconry show in season

items.season: April to November for the shows; in June the town holds its medieval festival.

items.title: Auvers-sur-Oise
items.transit: Gare du Nord → Auvers-sur-Oise, about 1h with a change at Pontoise; direct trains at weekends in season
items.why: Van Gogh spent the last seventy days of his life here and painted seventy-five canvases. The village has barely changed: you can stand in the wheatfield he painted the crows over, see the church from the picture, climb the stairs to the tiny attic room he died in, and visit his grave beside his brother's. It is a strange, quiet, moving day out and it costs almost nothing.

stops.text: The Auberge Ravoux and Van Gogh's attic room
The church from the painting
The wheatfield of the crows, above the village
Vincent and Theo's graves side by side
Daubigny's house and studio

items.season: April to October, when the Van Gogh house is open. Weekends bring direct trains in season.

items.title: Fontainebleau & the Forest
items.transit: Gare de Lyon → Fontainebleau-Avon, ~40 min, then bus 1
items.why: A royal palace lived in continuously for eight centuries — more interesting and far emptier than Versailles — inside a 25,000-hectare forest of sandstone boulders that is one of the birthplaces of rock climbing. Do the château in the morning and walk in the forest after, or skip the château entirely and just walk. Autumn is the best season for it.

stops.text: Gare de Lyon to Fontainebleau-Avon, then bus 1
The château: the Renaissance gallery of François I
The Jardin anglais and the carp pond
The forest after lunch — the Gorges de Franchard or the boulders at Bas-Bréau

items.season: All year; autumn in the forest is the best. The château is shut on Tuesdays.

items.title: Giverny — Monet's Garden
items.transit: Gare Saint-Lazare → Vernon-Giverny (~50 min), then the shuttle bus
items.why: The actual garden, the actual water-lily pond, the actual green bridge. Open roughly April to the start of November only. Go on a weekday and be at the gate when it opens, because by 11:00 it is shoulder to shoulder and the whole point is the quiet. The Musée des Impressionnismes next door is a good, near-empty second stop.

stops.text: Saint-Lazare to Vernon-Giverny, then the shuttle
Monet's garden when the gates open
The water garden and the Japanese bridge
The Musée des Impressionnismes next door
Or hire a bike in Vernon and cycle the path to Giverny

items.season: April to the start of November only. May and June for the flowers; September for the light.

items.title: Versailles
items.transit: M5 to Gare d'Austerlitz then RER C, or RER B to Saint-Michel and change
items.why: Worth doing once, but do it properly and against the grain: skip the state apartments queue, go straight to the gardens and the Trianon estate, and see Marie-Antoinette's hamlet, which is a fake rustic village with a working farm and is far stranger and better than the palace. On summer weekends the fountains run to music, and the night fountain shows run through September.

stops.text: RER C to Versailles-Château
Straight to the gardens
The Grand and Petit Trianon
Marie-Antoinette's hamlet
The Hall of Mirrors late in the day, when the queue has gone

items.season: April to October for the fountains and gardens; the palace is shut on Mondays.

items.title: Parc de Sceaux
items.transit: RER B to Parc de Sceaux or Bourg-la-Reine
items.why: A vast free Le Nôtre park with canals and terraces, forty-five minutes out on the RER B. The real reason to go is the first two weeks of April, when the Japanese cherry orchard in the Bosquet Nord flowers all at once and the whole thing turns pink — it is the best hanami in the Paris region and it is free. Set a reminder for late March.

stops.text: RER B to Parc de Sceaux
The cherry orchard in the Bosquet Nord
The Grandes Cascades and the Octagon
Picnic on the lawns

items.season: The first two weeks of April for the cherry blossom; any sunny weekend otherwise.

items.title: Senlis
items.transit: Gare du Nord → Chantilly, then the bus to Senlis
items.why: A small medieval town of cobbled lanes and a Gothic cathedral, with Roman walls and a ruined royal castle, that almost no visitor to Paris reaches because there is no direct train. Combine it with Chantilly in one day — same line, and the bus between them takes twenty minutes. Very good in autumn.

stops.text: Gare du Nord to Chantilly, then the bus
The cathedral of Notre-Dame
The Roman walls and the ruined royal castle
The cobbled lanes of the old town
Back via Chantilly

items.season: All year; very good in autumn.

items.title: Meaux
items.transit: Gare de l'Est → Meaux, about 25 min
items.why: Twenty-five minutes from Gare de l'Est, and the home of Brie de Meaux. A Gothic cathedral, an episcopal palace with a garden laid out by Le Nôtre in the shape of a bishop's mitre, and cheese-makers you can visit. Add the Musée de la Grande Guerre, one of the best First World War museums in Europe, if that interests you. A good half-day when you want out of the city without a project.

stops.text: Gare de l’Est, 25 minutes
The cathedral and the bishop’s palace
Brie de Meaux at a cheese shop
The Musée de la Grande Guerre

items.title: Saint-Germain-en-Laye
items.priceNote: ~€8 return · château free on some days
items.transit: RER A direct, about 35 min from Châtelet
items.why: The easiest half-day escape: one RER, no changes, and you step out into a château that is now the national archaeology museum, with a 2.4 km stone terrace by Le Nôtre looking back over the whole of Paris. The forest behind it is enormous. Good for an afternoon when you want trees and a view without committing to a whole day.

stops.text: RER A to the end of the line
The château and the national archaeology museum
The Grande Terrasse, looking back over Paris
The forest behind

items.season: All year; sunset from the terrace is the reason.

items.title: Chartres
items.why: The finest medieval stained glass anywhere in the world, almost all of it original 13th-century, in a cathedral that survived both wars intact. The blue is a colour nobody has since managed to reproduce. From April to October the whole town is lit with projections after dark under the Chartres en Lumières programme, which makes an evening return worth it.

stops.text: Montparnasse to Chartres
The cathedral: the blue windows and the labyrinth on the floor
Down to the lower town and the river Eure
Stay for Chartres en Lumières after dark, April to early January

items.season: All year; the light shows run from April into winter.

items.title: The Loire châteaux: Chenonceau and Amboise
items.transit: TGV from Montparnasse to Saint-Pierre-des-Corps, about 1 h, then the TER or a hire car
items.why: The Loire valley is an hour from Montparnasse, and two châteaux make a full day: Chenonceau, built across the river Cher on arches, the most beautiful house in France; and Amboise, above the town, where Leonardo da Vinci spent his last years at the manor of Clos Lucé down the street. Chambord, the biggest, is better as a second day.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours

stops.text: TGV to Saint-Pierre-des-Corps; pick up a car or the train to Chenonceaux
Chenonceau when it opens — walk the long gallery over the river
Lunch in Amboise, with a glass of Vouvray
Château d’Amboise and the chapel where Leonardo is buried
Clos Lucé, his last house, with models of his machines in the garden

items.season: April to October; Chenonceau is lovely in the autumn mist. Book trains early for the cheap fares.

items.title: Mont-Saint-Michel
items.priceNote: The abbey ~€13; stay the night on or near the mount
items.transit: TGV to Rennes, about 1 h 30, then the direct coach, about 1 h 10 — a weekend
items.why: An abbey on a rock in a bay whose tide comes in, as Victor Hugo said, at the speed of a galloping horse. By day the one street is a crush; the trick is to sleep there, or nearby, and see it at dusk and dawn with the day-trippers gone. Walk out across the sands only with a certified guide: the quicksand and the tide are real.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours

stops.text: TGV to Rennes and the coach to the mount
The abbey at the top, and the cloister hanging over the bay
An omelette at La Mère Poulard, if you must
The mount at dusk from the causeway, when the lights come on
Next morning, a guided walk across the bay at low tide

items.season: All year. The spring and autumn equinox tides are the most dramatic; winter is empty and wild.

items.title: Étretat and the Alabaster Coast
items.priceNote: Train ~€40–70 return; the cliffs are free
items.transit: Train from Saint-Lazare to Le Havre, about 2 h, then the bus, about 1 h
items.why: The white chalk cliffs Monet painted over and over: a natural arch standing in the sea, a needle of rock beside it, and cliff-top paths on both sides of a pebble beach. Walk up the Falaise d'Aval to look down on the arch, then across to the chapel on the Falaise d'Amont. Pair it with Le Havre, the concrete city Auguste Perret rebuilt, which is a World Heritage site.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours

stops.text: Train to Le Havre, then the bus along the coast
Up the Falaise d'Aval to the arch and the Aiguille
Across the beach and up the Falaise d'Amont to the chapel
Moules or oysters on the seafront
Le Havre on the way home: the Perret church of Saint-Joseph and the MuMa's Impressionists

items.season: April to October. Check the tides: some of the beach walks are cut off at high water.

items.title: Lille
items.transit: TGV from Gare du Nord, about 1 h
items.why: A Flemish city an hour north, and a different country in all but name: gabled brick houses, beer rather than wine, waffles, and a Grand'Place ringed with baroque. The Palais des Beaux-Arts is one of the best museums in France outside Paris. And twenty minutes away by tram, La Piscine in Roubaix is an art museum inside an Art Deco swimming pool.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours

stops.text: TGV to Lille-Flandres
The Grand'Place and the Vieille Bourse courtyard of second-hand booksellers
Méert's filled waffles, since 1761
The Palais des Beaux-Arts
La Piscine in Roubaix by tram — the museum in a swimming pool

items.season: All year; the Braderie, Europe's biggest flea market, fills the city on the first weekend of September.

items.title: Rouen
items.why: The Norman capital, an hour down the Seine: a whole old town of timber-framed houses, the cathedral Monet painted thirty times at different hours of the day, and the square where Joan of Arc was burned in 1431. It is the best-preserved medieval city centre within easy reach of Paris, and the Musée des Beaux-Arts is free.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours

stops.text: Train from Saint-Lazare
The cathedral — find the spot Monet painted it from
Rue du Gros-Horloge, under the great clock
Place du Vieux-Marché and the modern church of Joan of Arc
The Musée des Beaux-Arts, free, with a Monet cathedral inside

items.season: All year; the cathedral is lit with projections on summer nights.
